adults.title: The Giving Path
adults.big_idea: The Savior's path is a giving path, so we put gambling out of our lives entirely and use the time and means we save to do good.
adults.objective: Learners will be able to explain in their own words why gambling is contrary to the Savior's giving path, and will choose one specific good cause for their time or means this week.
prepare: Read President Christofferson's talk, especially the paragraphs on opportunity cost, example, and living on a higher plane (T08.14–16 and T08.22–25).
Read 1 Corinthians 8:9–11, Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and 3 Nephi 12:6.
Write on the board before class: “Where will this lead?”
Bring a half sheet of paper and a pen for each learner.
Pray for anyone in the room who may be quietly carrying this burden, personally or in the family. Plan to teach principles and never ask for disclosures.

segments.name: A wise friend's questions
steps: Begin with prayer. Point to the question on the board and explain that President Christofferson, quoting President Oaks, asked us to put it to our present choices.
Give a brief hypothetical: a good man, in no one's ward, starts putting a few dollars on weekend games from his phone. His friends all do it. He calls it harmless fun.
Ask learners to turn to a neighbor for one minute and name the questions a wise, loving friend might ask him.
Take three or four answers and list them on the board. Say that President Christofferson spoke to us as that kind of friend, with what he called a sense of duty.
questions: What would a friend who loved him want him to think about?

segments.name: Why it is wrong, in his words
steps: Form groups of three or four. Ask each group to read the paragraph that begins with the fact that gambling is morally wrong (T08.22) and find every reason President Christofferson gives.
Have groups call out what they found while you list it: the desire for something for nothing; gain that comes at others' expense; our resources are stewardships; it builds nothing of value.
Ask one learner to read Matthew 22:39. Invite the class to connect the commandment to the list on the board.
Read aloud President Oaks's statement about the giving path and the taking path (aligned quote, T08.23).
questions: Which of these reasons would you most want your own family to understand, and why?
How does asking whether a purchase builds anything change the way you look at your spending?

segments.name: Counting the opportunity cost
steps: Read President Christofferson's three questions about opportunity cost (key quote, T08.14).

Hand out paper. Ask learners to draw a line down the middle and write, in silence for two minutes, what a habit of wagering takes on the left under four words: money, time, relationships, worthwhile pursuits. Tell them they may also think of any pursuit of their own that takes without building.
On the right, have them write what the same hours and dollars could build instead.
Invite two or three to share one line from the right-hand column only.
questions: What did you notice when you saw the two columns side by side?

segments.name: Who is watching me?
steps: Briefly retell Paul's counsel as the talk does: a believer firm in Christ could eat food that had been offered to idols as nothing more than a meal, yet Paul cautioned the disciples to abstain so that a weaker brother would not be led astray.
Read 1 Corinthians 8:9–11 in pairs and look for whom Paul is protecting.
Read the key quote about a little gambling being more costly to those who follow our example (T08.16). Point out that President Christofferson names our children and also others we may not know.
Discuss the questions. Let learners carry the conversation.
questions: When have you gladly given up something you felt free to do because of someone who was watching you?
What does it do to our choices to remember that Christ died for that person as He did for us?

segments.name: A higher plane
steps: Read President Christofferson's plea to live on a higher plane and his description of a life well-lived (T08.24).
Read his invitation (T08.25): not only to refrain, but to use the time and resources saved for doing good.

Ask half the class to read Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and half to read 3 Nephi 12:6. Have each half tell the other what the Lord asks and what He promises. Draw out the promise the talk quotes: those who hunger and thirst after righteousness are filled with the Holy Ghost.
Share Elder Soares's words about fast offerings (aligned quote) as one example of the giving path already within everyone's reach.
questions: What good cause have you been meaning to give more of yourself to?

segments.name: Choose and follow up
steps: Check for understanding: ask one learner to say in a sentence why gambling leads away from the Savior's path, and another to add what the speaker asked us to do with what we save.
Invite everyone to circle one line on the right side of their paper and write next to it a day this week.
Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking two or three people what good they did with an hour or a few dollars they redirected.
Close with your testimony that the Savior's way is the giving way and that He fills those who hunger for righteousness. End with President Christofferson's closing words from Jacob: “O be wise.”

key_quotes.text: What is the opportunity cost of gambling? What do you forgo in terms of money, time, relationships, and worthwhile pursuits? Where does it lead?
A little gambling that seemingly has only a minor impact in your life may be more costly to them if they take license from your example.

Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing. Its structure requires that any gain comes at others’ expense. It’s hard to reconcile that with the commandment to love our neighbor as ourselves.
A key part of a life well-lived is contributing to the well-being of others. It is being productive in worthy endeavors. It is being and doing better without others doing worse.

scriptures.use: Read in pairs in the fourth segment; look for whom Paul is protecting and why that person matters so much to the Savior.
One learner reads it aloud in the second segment; the class connects it to the speaker's reasons listed on the board.
Half the class reads it in the fifth segment and reports what the Lord asks of us.
The other half reads it in the fifth segment and reports the promised blessing; attach the closing invitation to this promise.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: The attitude of taking something from someone else in order to enhance our own position—[which is] the essence of gambling—leads us away from the giving path of Christ and toward the taking path of the adversary.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Soares
aligned_quotes.text: Though our fast offerings may seem small and simple, they become consecrated expressions of compassion, concern, and service.

invitations.text: my plea again is not only to refrain from gambling but to use the time and resources saved thereby for doing good
Today, I am pleading with all of us to live life on a higher plane.

takeaways: Gambling seeks something for nothing at another's expense; the Savior's path is the giving path.
My choices are a guide to others, and every one of them is a soul for whom Christ died.
The Lord fills with the Holy Ghost those who hunger and thirst after righteousness.
act: Decide, and say to your family, that wagers of any size have no place in your life, including small ones made for fun.
Name one hour and one small sum this week and give them on purpose to a good cause: a visit, a fast offering, a neighbor's need.
Ask of one regular use of your time or money this week where it leads, and write your answer.
Talk with your children or grandchildren about what President Christofferson taught, and listen to what they are seeing among their friends.
music: Because I Have Been Given Much
adapt: At home with adults: skip the groups. Read T08.22 and T08.24 aloud together, do the two-column page at the table, and share one line each.
Short on time: keep the two-column writing and the higher plane segment; summarize Paul's counsel in two sentences.
If someone raises a personal or family struggle, thank them, keep the class on the principles, and offer to talk privately afterward. The bishop can help.

youth.title: Who Really Wins?
youth.big_idea: Gambling takes and builds nothing; the Savior invites us to a higher plane where we use our time and means to give and do good.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain why gambling is wrong and what it costs, practice a confident answer to an invitation to bet, and choose one way to use their time or money for good this week.
prepare: Read President Christofferson's talk. Mark T08.07, T08.09–10, T08.14–16 and T08.22–25.
Write three questions on separate cards for the group work in the third segment (see the steps there).
Bring paper and pens. Ask youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app open.
Decide beforehand that no one will be asked whether they or anyone they know has gambled. Teach the principles and keep the room safe.

segments.name: Closest guess
steps: As youth walk in, split them into two or three teams and give each a sheet of paper. Start right away.

Ask three questions from the talk. Teams write a guess for each and hold it up; the closest guess scores a point. One: in the United States, what percent of boys age 11 to 17 reported gambling last year? (36.) Two: what was the percent at age 17? (49, virtually half.) Three: how much did the global gambling industry take in during 2025? (An estimated 758 billion dollars.)
Ask where that money came from. Then read the key quote from T08.07 about the industry's business model.
Say that President Christofferson of the First Presidency said he spoke about this from a sense of duty, and that he said youth and young adults are affected more than others.
questions: If the whole business only works when its customers lose, who really wins?

segments.name: Why it finds us
steps: Have youth open the talk on their phones and read T08.09 silently. Ask them to find every reason President Christofferson gives that their age group is hit harder.
List what they find on the board: impulsivity, peer influence, early exposure, easy online access, intense marketing, wide social acceptance.
Ask the first question below. Accept general answers such as ads, apps, group chats and sports talk. Do not ask for names or personal stories.
Point out what he says it does: it robs time from studies, relationships and career development, and it crowds out things of value.
questions: Without naming anyone, where do people your age run into this?
Which item on this list do you think is the strongest pull, and why?

segments.name: Three honest questions
steps: Form three groups and give each a card. Card 1: It is only a few dollars and it is fun, so what is the harm? Read T08.14 and T08.11. Card 2: I can handle it, so why does it matter what I do? Read T08.15–16 and 1 Corinthians 8:9–11. Card 3: It is legal in lots of places, so why is it wrong? Read T08.22–23 and Matthew 22:39.
Give groups three minutes to find President Christofferson's answer and put it in their own words in two sentences.
Each group reports in one minute. After group 1, write “opportunity cost” on the board with the four things he names: money, time, relationships, worthwhile pursuits.
After group 3, read President Oaks's words about the giving path and the taking path (aligned quote, T08.23).
questions: Which answer would actually make sense to a friend who is not a member of the Church?

segments.name: Say it out loud
steps: Set a hypothetical: a group chat is putting five dollars each on tonight's game, and a friend tags you to join.
In pairs, youth take turns being the friend and giving a reply that is short, kind and confident, with no lecture. One minute each.
Ask a few pairs to share their best line. Write two or three on the board.
Read Elder Andersen's sentence on spiritual courage (aligned quote). Remind them of President Christofferson's point that others who are newer or weaker in the faith may be watching what they do.
questions: What makes a no easier to say, and easier for a friend to hear?

segments.name: Trade up
steps: Read President Christofferson's invitation (T08.25). Point out that he asks for two things: to refrain, and to use the time and resources saved for doing good.
Have one youth read Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and another read 3 Nephi 12:6. Ask what the Lord promises to those who hunger and thirst after righteousness.
Read the key quote from T08.24 about a life well-lived.

Give two minutes of silent writing, on paper or in a phone note: if you had one extra hour and ten dollars this week, list three ways you could use them to build something in yourself, your family or someone near you. Then have each youth star one.
questions: What is the difference between getting ahead and getting ahead without anyone else doing worse?

segments.name: Choose and follow up
steps: Check for understanding: go around the room and have each youth finish the sentence aloud: Gambling is wrong because… or Instead I will…

Invite each youth to do their starred idea before next Sunday. Promise, in the words the talk quotes from the Savior, that those who hunger and thirst after righteousness are filled with the Holy Ghost.
Tell them you will open next week by asking what they traded up to, and that you will share yours first.
Bear a brief testimony that the Savior gave everything for each of us, and that His way is the giving way. Close with Jacob's words that President Christofferson ended with: “O be wise.”

key_quotes.text: Simply put, the industry’s entire business model is built on its customers losing money.
It robs time from studies, relationships, and career development. It crowds out things of value and in their place fosters greed.
Every soul is precious, and Christ died for him, for her, as He did for you.
It is being and doing better without others doing worse.

scriptures.use: Group 2 reads it in the third segment to answer why my example matters even if I think I can handle it.
Group 3 reads it in the third segment and explains how winning at someone else's expense fits, or does not fit, this commandment.
One youth reads it aloud in the Trade up segment before the silent writing; ask what a good cause looks like this week.
One youth reads it aloud in the Trade up segment; identify the promise and attach it to the closing invitation.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: The attitude of taking something from someone else in order to enhance our own position—[which is] the essence of gambling—leads us away from the giving path of Christ and toward the taking path of the adversary.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Andersen
aligned_quotes.text: Spiritual courage is the triumph over obstacles, doubt, and fear in choosing the right.

invitations.text: my plea again is not only to refrain from gambling but to use the time and resources saved thereby for doing good
Today, I am pleading with all of us to live life on a higher plane.

takeaways: Gambling only works when people lose; it takes and builds nothing.
Someone is watching what I do, and Christ died for that person too.
The Lord asks me to trade up: to spend my time and money on good causes, and He promises the Holy Ghost.
act: Do your starred idea: one hour and a little money spent on purpose to build something good.
Decide your answer now for the next time someone invites you to bet, and keep it ready.
Delete or mute one app, account or chat that keeps putting betting in front of you.
If this has already become hard to stop, talk with a parent or your bishop this week. They will be glad you came.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip the teams. Guess the numbers together, take the three cards one at a time, and do the role play parent to youth, then switch.
Short on time: keep Closest guess, the three cards and Trade up; drop the role play and give its scenario as the week's challenge.
If a youth shares something personal, thank them, do not press for detail in front of the class, and follow up privately with kindness.

children.title: Jesus's Giving Way
children.big_idea: I am happy when I work, share and give, the way Jesus does.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Jesus's way is to work, share and give, and will choose one way to do good for someone this week.
prepare: Bring building blocks (or paper cups that stack), plain paper, and crayons.
Read Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and Matthew 22:39.
Practice the three actions: work (pound one fist on the other), share (hold both hands out), give (hands on heart, then open them outward).
This talk was about gambling. With children, teach only the hopeful truths underneath it; do not describe or explain betting.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Greet each child by name and invite a child to pray.
Sing “Kindness Begins with Me” together, once seated and once standing.
Ask the question below and listen to three or four answers.
questions: When did you help someone or share something, and how did you feel inside?

segments.name: Two towers
steps: Make two small piles of blocks in front of you, one for each hand. Say you want the first pile to be bigger, then move blocks from the second pile onto the first until the second is almost gone.
Ask the first question below. Help the children see that one pile only grew because the other pile lost.
Now give every child one or two blocks. Invite them to come up one at a time and add their blocks to build one tall tower together.
Ask the second question. Say: Jesus does not take. Jesus gives. His way is the giving way.
questions: My first pile got bigger. What happened to the other pile? Was that fair?
How was building the tower together different?

segments.name: Work, share, give
steps: Have the children stand. Teach the short truth with actions: I can work (pound fists), share (hands out), and give (hands on heart, then open).
Say it together three times: once in a normal voice, once in a whisper, once in a strong voice.
Let a child lead it one more time.

segments.name: Busy doing good
steps: Open the scriptures to Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and tell the children the Lord asks us to “be anxiously engaged in a good cause.” Explain that this means being busy and glad to do good things.

Play Show Me: call out a good thing and have the children act it out without words. Set the table. Pick up toys. Help someone who dropped their books. Draw a picture for a friend. Take turns with the ball.
Let two or three children think of a good thing for everyone to act out.
Ask the question below.
questions: Who is happy when you do these things?

segments.name: What I have, I can use for good
steps: Hold up your two hands, then point to a clock, then hold up one crayon. Say: Heavenly Father has given me hands, time, and things. He trusts me to use them to do good.
Hold up the hands again and ask what good hands can do. Do the same for time and for the crayon.
Tell the children that at general conference President Christofferson, who serves in the First Presidency, taught that a big part of a good life is helping others be well and happy.
Read Matthew 22:39 from the scriptures, or tell it simply: Jesus asks us to love other people as we love ourselves.
questions: What good can you do with your hands? With ten minutes? With one crayon?

segments.name: A gift I made
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Help them fold the paper in half like a card.
Invite them to draw something kind for a person they choose, and to give the card to that person. This is working and giving at the same time.
As they draw, walk around and ask each child who the card is for and what else they could do for that person this week.
Have the children hold up their cards. Thank them for their work.

segments.name: Reach higher
steps: Have the children stand and reach as high as they can on their toes. Tell them President Christofferson asked all of us to live on a higher plane. That means choosing Jesus's giving way.
Check what they learned: ask what Jesus's way is, and do the three actions together one last time.
Tell them the prophet Jacob in the Book of Mormon said, “O be wise.” Have them whisper it back to you. Say: we are wise when we follow Jesus.

Invite each child to give their card and do one helping thing this week. Tell them you will ask next week what they did. Share your testimony that Jesus loves them and gives to them every day, and close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: A key part of a life well-lived is contributing to the well-being of others.
It is being and doing better without others doing worse.
O be wise; what can I say more?

scriptures.use: Open to it in the Busy doing good segment; say the phrase the talk quotes and let children act out good causes.
Read or tell it simply in the fifth segment: Jesus asks us to love others as we love ourselves.
In the closing, tell the children Jacob's three short words and have them whisper the words back.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Marion G. Romney, quoted by Elder Fantone
aligned_quotes.text: Service is the very fiber of which an exalted life in the celestial kingdom is made

invitations.text: Today, I am pleading with all of us to live life on a higher plane.

takeaways: Jesus's way is the giving way.
I can work, share and give.
Heavenly Father trusts me to use what I have to do good.
act: Give the card you made to the person you made it for.
Do one helping job at home without being asked.
Share something of yours with a brother, sister or friend.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep each part short and repeat the work, share, give actions between activities. Let helpers hand out blocks and crayons. Skip reading the verses; say each idea in one sentence. In Show Me, do each action with them. Sing the song again if they grow restless.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have a child read Doctrine and Covenants 58:27 and Matthew 22:39 aloud and tell what a good cause is. After the two towers, ask why getting more by making someone else lose is not Jesus's way. Let an older child lead Show Me, and read the sentence about service from President Marion G. Romney, which Elder Fantone quoted, and ask what it means.
